title: Incorporating New Generation Cold-Formed High-Strength Steel (CFHSS) to the Conformity of Present Product Standards
abstract: Abstract Cold-formed high-strength steel (CFHSS) has been gaining popularity in the construction industry due to its high strength-to-weight ratio. CFHSS is produced with a nominal yield strength of 460 MPa and above, in compliance with the national steel product standard, to assure safety, durability, and quality in use in construction. However, owing to the rapid global production of steel products, a wide range of steel products from different countries, described as ‘foreign steel’, have been shipped worldwide. These steel products have created an imbalance between design guidelines and product standards that differ by country, resulting in unpredictable construction outcomes. The Eurocode 3 and American Standard AISI S100 design codes of practice authorise the use of steel that fulfils the product standards for mechanical and chemical properties, as verified by testing procedure. However, existing steel product standards from Europe, America, Australia, Japan, and Malaysia only deal with steel with a tensile strength of up to 550 MPa. Hence, alternative approach to employ higher grades CFHSS in structural steel design was addressed.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In recent years, high-strength steel (HSS) has gained significant traction in the construction sector due to its exceptional combination of low weight and remarkable strength. HSS is typically classified as a steel with a nominal yield strength,  f y , of 460 MPa and above. To ensure its applicability in construction, HSS is fabricated to comply with national steel product standards (Standards Australia Limited [SAL],  52 ; ASTM International [ASTM],  4 ; British Standards Institution [BSI],  14 ; Japanese Standards Association [JSA],  30 ; and Department of Standards Malaysia [DSM], 19 ), assuring compliance with safety, durability and quality requirements. HSS has several uses in construction. Its higher yield strength compared to traditional mild steel allows for significantly enhanced load-carrying capacity, enabling the development of large and spacious structures and minimising construction costs. Bridges, skyscrapers, warehouses and complexes have been built using HSS with steel grades ranging from 460 MPa to 800 MPa (Ban & Shi,  6 ).

The cold reduction process is one method of producing HSS; the steel it produces is known as cold-formed high-strength steel (CFHSS). In the reduction mill, the steel sheet’s thickness is reduced by the cold reduction process until the desired thickness is reached. This milling procedure lengthens the grain structure in the milling direction, increasing the steel’s material strength while decreasing its ductility (Rogers & Hancock,  44 ). The resulting decrease in ductility has caused concerns about using CFHSS for structural applications, which can be severely affected by stress concentrations when subjected to loading. As a result, a ductility criterion has been added to the design standards EN 1993-1-1:2005 (BSI,  8 ) and AISI S100-16 (American Iron and Steel Institute,  3 ) to address the problem. Although the design standards include this criterion, using steel that complies with the certified steel delivery product standards also ensure adherence to the required ductility provisions.

All structural steel employed in construction must comply with the relevant product standards for its specification to ensure legitimacy and safety in practice. These product standards correspond with the design codes of their respective countries, thereby avoiding discrepancies in design concepts. According to Chung et al. ( 18 ), China accounts for 52.1% of the world’s annual steel production. This figure, reported by the World Steel Association, which represents approximately 85% of global steel production. Despite complying with their respective national standards, these foreign steel products are regarded as non-conforming under Eurocode because their product specifications and tolerances differ from those prescribed in Eurocode. In Malaysia, however, the Uniform Building By-Laws (UBBL) require that all building designs adhere to the national design codes which includes the design of steel structures to MS EN 1993 (Kementerian Perumahan dan Kerajaan Tempatan,  34 ), resulting in a conflict when foreign steel is introduced. This leads to a discrepancy between legal design obligations and the classification of non-conforming steel under Eurocode. Overcoming this limitation demands either broadening Eurocode conformity or harmonising international steel product standards. In Singapore, the Building and Construction Authority (BCA,  7 ) has already implemented guidelines to harmonise foreign steel standards with Eurocode provisions, demonstrating a practical pathway to enhanced standardisation.

The Eurocode has released a design standard that raises the current permissible steel strength from S 460 (BSI,  8 ) to S 700 MC (BSI,  10 ), allowing for the use of higher steel grades. However, further research and investigation into the product standards (SAL,  52 ; ASTM, 4 ; BSI,  14 ; JSA,  30 ; DSM,  19 ) has revealed that the highest available steel grades for cold-formed steel coil have a yield strength of only 550 MPa. In the automobile sector, advanced high-strength steel (AHSS) is widely used, where the yield strength of which can exceed 1000 MPa. The AHSS family currently contains over 20 steel grades, and it is still evolving today (Keeler et al.,  33 ). Despite the AHSS family’s exceptionally high steel grades, its integration in the construction sector remains unexplored. Recently, tensile testing and numerical analysis have been carried out to investigate the mechanical performance of AHSS when used as connections in construction (Ding et al.,  20 ,  21 ,  22 ; Xia et al.,  55 ). However, there has been little study of AHSS’s conformity with local product standards for structural steel design.

sections.heading: Eurocode (EN 1993-1-3)
paragraphs: In Europe and most Asian countries, the regulatory body code of practice for cold-formed steel design is Eurocode EN 1993-1-3:2006. Table 3.1a and 3.1b of EN 1993-1-3 list the standard basic yield strength ( f y ) and ultimate strength ( f u ) of different steel types. This code of practice applies to steel with a core thickness between 0.45 mm and 15 mm for use in sheeting or members, with grades generally ranging from S 235 to S 460. Although BS EN 10149-1 (BSI,  11 ) permits the usage of steel graded up to S 700 MC, the minimum thickness of the steel is only 1.5 mm, as shown in EN 1993-1-12, Table  2 . Nevertheless, the inclusion of other steel grades is possible, as stated in BS EN 1993-1-1, Cl. 3.2.1. For a new steel grade to be included, its mechanical property must conform to the ductility requirement stated in EN 1993-1-1. For CFHSS, which has a yield strength equivalent to steel grade S 700, EN 1993-1-12 requires a tensile strength to yield strength ratio  f u / f y  >1.05, elongation at failure  A  > 10% and ultimate strain  ε u  > 15  f y /E , as summarised in Table  1 .

sections.heading: American Standard (AISI S100)
paragraphs: The American Iron and Steel Institute has published the North American Specification for the Design of Cold-formed Steel Structural Members, which permits the usage of steel types other than those specified in the standard if the steel fulfils the requirements stated in clause A3.2. Firstly, the steel’s thickness should be less than 25.4 mm. Secondly, the design yield stress should be determined by either a full section tensile test to ASTM A370, stub column test to AISI S902, or calculated employing equation A3.3.2-1. The standard tensile coupon tests should be carried out for flat products as stated in clause K2.3.2, where a minimum of four tensile specimens shall be taken longitudinally from the master coil, stated in clause K2.3.3. Thirdly, the ductility requirements state that 12.7 mm gauge steel should be capable of local elongation of 20% and uniform elongation of more than 3% at fracture. When foreign steels have inadequate ductility, such as a maximum elongation lower than 3% or an  f u /f y  ratio lower than 1.08, designs incorporating them must treat their minimum tensile strength as a factor of 0.75 lower than that specified or 427 MPa, whichever is lower. Otherwise, this inadequate steel material should only be used in purlins, girts, and wall studs.

sections.heading: Steel Coil Standard Specification
paragraphs: Table  2  compares current steel coil standard specifications from different countries, specifically their structural properties requirements. In general, all standards cover steel grades up to 550 MPa. Their ductility requirements for elongation at fracture range from 2 to 16%, with a minimum  f u / f y  ratio of 1.02. Plastic strain at ultimate,  ε u , is currently not included in the Australian, American, or Japanese standards, whereas in EN 10,346, there is no minimum requirement for high-strength steel grades such as S 550 GD or HX 500 LAD. In countries such as Africa and Southeast Asia, where construction steel must be imported, the steel used for cold-formed steel coil production and the code of practice applied in design can be from different countries. Consequently, the designer should check these steel material properties, especially the plastic strain at fracture, for compliance with the local code of practice requirements before employing the CFHSS in structural design.

sections.heading: Current Research Studies on CFHSS
paragraphs: Research publications related to high-strength steel from the past 20 years have been studied to provide insight into the current development of CFHSS. The grades of high-strength steel were between 600 MPa and 850 MPa, with  f u / f y  ratios ranging from 1.01 to 1.25 and thickness ranging from 0.4 mm to 10 mm. Figure  1  shows the achieved elongation of the CFHSS, which ranged from 3 to 22%. As shown in Fig.  1 , studies have proven that certain CFHSS can achieve a strength of up to 850 MPa with adequate elongation, highlighting the need to update product standards to incorporate high-strength CFHSS.
Fig. 1 Range of steel studied in the literature review

Table  3  breaks down the content of the literature studied in this review, which covered 40 papers published in the last two decades with a focus on high-strength steel research. These were categorised into review or research papers and according to the types of high-strength steel applications on which they focused. Most of the research dealt with dual-phase steel from the AHSS family, martensitic steel (Singh et al.,  50 ; Elveli et al.,  23 ; Foroughi & Schafer,  24 ; Gruben et al.,  28 ) and conventional high-strength low-alloy steel (Zhu et al.,  61 ; Afkhami et al.,  1 ). As shown in Fig.  2 , these steel types have lower elongations at fracture than other steel types, and their  f u / f y  ratio can be as low as 1.10, as shown in Table  4 .

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties of CFHSS Material
paragraphs: The review of the current design standards revealed that most HSS did not meet the ductility criteria, as the  f y / f u  ratio of most structural steels studied was more than 0.85 (see Fig.  3 [b]), nor did they meet the plastic design guidelines, as their elongation percentage after fracture,  A t , was below 20%, as shown in Fig.  3 (a). A comparison of coupon test results for different steel grades, as shown in Fig.  3 (b), indicates that an increase in HSS’s yield strength,  f y , is associated with reduced ductility. However, there is still the possibility of manufacturing steel with a strength of more than 690 MPa and a maximum elongation of close to 20%, though this is subject to material and manufacturing factors.
Fig. 3 Summary of coupon test results from Tsinghua University (Ban & Shi, 6 )

Ma et al. ( 37 ) carried out tensile coupon tests of hollow flat, corner, and curved specimens of cold-formed high-strength steel with yield strengths of 700 MPa and 900 MPa. The test results were used to calibrate the newly developed stress-strain relationship model modified based on the Ramberg-Osgood model (Xia et al.,  55 ). Additionally, Afkhami et al. ( 1 ) evaluated the weldability of S 700 MC and S 1100 grade CFHSS via microstructural analysis, hardness measurement, tensile test and Charpy impact test. They found that although cold-formed S 700 MC had acceptable weldability, excessive deformation and pre-strains could result in premature failures in CFHSS joints. Hence, the bending and pre-straining criteria provided by the manufacturer must be checked to ensure the material’s suitability. Cheng et al. ( 17 ,  54 ) investigated the effect of grain size and precipitation on the microstructure and strength of high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). They found that a 550 MPa yield strength and 13% elongation can be achieved with Ti and V micro-alloyed steel, and the annealing temperature had an impact on the microstructure and mechanical properties of CFHSS.

sections.heading: Structural Strength of CFHSS Members
paragraphs: A notable research project on CFHSS was conducted at Johns Hopkins University, in which dual phase and martensitic AHSS were tested for use as connections, beams and columns. According to Ding et al. ( 22 ) the results were compared to the AISI’s predictions using the direct strength method (DSM). Their experimental results found that assuming a strength reduction factor of 0.78 to 0.98 from the manufacturer’s specifications was necessary for safe column design; the necessary reduction ratio was 0.77 for safe flexural beam design. They also discovered that true fracture strain can be a useful parameter for assessing steel ductility, local-distortional buckling interaction should be considered a separate limit state in beam design, and a DSM distortional curve should be developed when designing an AHSS column. These experimental outcomes agreed with Foroughi and Schafer’s ( 24 ) parametric numerical simulation study, which suggested that local-global interaction does not accurately capture the strength of longer CFHSS members and that distortional-global interaction also requires further research.

Researchers have also investigated the net cross-section resistance of S 690 bolted connections and statistically analysed the test results to compare them with the current design codes of practice (Može et al.,  40 ). Although their net section failure results indicated that CFHSS was ductile and comparable to mild steels, the study also indicated that net-section checking was crucial as yielding of the gross section was restricted by a low  f u / f y  ratio.

sections.heading: Standards for and Product Certification of Foreign Steel
paragraphs: The literature review shows that the accepted range of product standards in the Eurocode design standard covers a yield strength of 180 MPa to 960 MPa with a required  f u /f y  ratio above 1.05 and elongation at failure greater than 10% (BSI,  8 ; BSI,  10 ). On the other hand, the AISI design standard includes steels with a yield strength between 170 MPa and 550 MPa, a  f u /f y  ratio of more than 1.08, and an elongation greater than 1% (American Iron and Steel Institute,  3 ). Both design standards permit the use of foreign steel that has been found suitable through testing and have established their own criteria for mechanical properties, specifically ductility. The review also found that the present product standards for cold-formed steel coils remain limited to steel with a maximum yield strength of 570 MPa, even though they allow for the design of higher-strength 960 MPa steel if its suitability is proven by testing, as shown in Table  2 .

Despite these constraints, several studies have explored CFHSS with yield strengths ranging from 602 MPa to 827 MPa and elongation after fracture ranging from 3% to 22%. Additionally, the ongoing development of AHSS for the automotive industry has resulted in materials with yield strengths ranging from 300 to 1250 MPa, ductility between 5% and 75%, and  f u /f y  from 1.10 to 2.10. An approach that expands the selection of high yield strength steel in product specifications is necessary to allow engineers to use new-generation CFHSS or AHSS in the future construction of innovative structures.

The guidelines published by Chung et al. ( 18 ) and Singapore’s Building and Construction Authority [BCA] ( 7 ) have attempted to harmonise foreign steel design standards with those of the Eurocode. Singapore has enforced the use of certified construction materials in accordance with BC1:2023 (BCA,  7 ) to ensure the safety of construction projects. Projects that wish to include new steel materials, including CFHSS plate, must refer to BC1 Table 2.3, where various experimental tests of the intended product, such as yield strength, tensile strength, elongation after fracture, impact energy, chemical content, and carbon equivalent value, are mandatory for product certification (BCA,  7 ). According to Chung et al. ( 18 ), these experimental results for the steel samples may be obtained by tensile testing to BS EN ISO 6892-1:2019 standard, Charpy impact testing to BS EN ISO 148-1:2010 standard, and chemical analysis to BS EN ISO 14284:2002 standard. A further requirement to ensure the test data is verified is to conduct the laboratory test at an ISO/IEC 17,025 accredited laboratory such as SINGLAS in Singapore and SIRIM in Malaysia. The handbook to BC1:2023 (BCA,  7 ) explains the criteria for the acceptance of evaluated steel, which consists of mechanical properties, ductility, impact toughness, chemical composition and dimensional and mass tolerances. BC1:2023 further states that the laboratory-tested strength of these foreign steels should be assumed to be at least 10% less during project design. The experimental test results, as well as the factory production control (FPC) information and manufacturer test certification (MTC), should be presented to local authorities for product certification. For countries other than Singapore, local legislative regulations for structural steel should be reviewed, and material requirements from the local code of practice can be used as guidance for the material certification of CFHSS. In accordance with BC1:2023 Clause 6.0, the criteria for evaluating the acceptance of steel product certification are based on the current standard and shall be updated in line with the most recent product standards, allowing for future developments in advanced materials such as CFHSS and AHSS to be certified and adopted in the construction industry.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: As the construction industry seeks higher-strength steel for lighter construction, the development of CFHSS could provide opportunities for more advanced structural projects. This review’s findings can be summarised as follows:

Although Eurocode 3 permits the design of CFHSS with a tensile strength in excess of 960 MPa, the current product standard for CFHSS steel coil is capped at 550 MPa in BS EN 10346:2015. Hence, it is essential to expand the steel coil product standard to incorporate higher steel strengths, as existing studies on CFHSS and AHSS have explored steels with tensile strengths greater than 550 MPa and mechanical properties that comply with Eurocode 3’s criteria. BC1 2012 enforces the use of certified steel material to ensure the safety, reliability, and market transparency of the steel products used in construction. For a material to be certified, it must have specific characteristics according to experimental tests by an accredited laboratory. The criteria for the approval of steel material may be further expanded once the latest steel delivery product standards are published, allowing CFHSS and AHSS to make an appearance in the construction market soon.

The development and usage of high-strength steels such as CFHSS must be acknowledged. It was suggested that the criteria for steel product certification be expanded to push the boundaries of future construction projects for advanced design concepts.
